lead: An amplifier needs a steady DC current and voltage before any signal arrives. A resistor network sets that point. Three standard networks are fixed bias, collector-to-base feedback bias and voltage divider bias. They differ in how far the collector current moves when β or temperature changes. Fixed bias moves most; the divider least. This chapter gives each circuit, its DC equations, stability factor and design steps.
prereq: You need the DC load line, the Q-point and the stability factor S from Chapter 2.1.

sections.h3: Fixed bias (base bias): one resistor, no feedback

blocks.text: R<sub>B</sub> runs from V<sub>CC</sub> to the base, R<sub>C</sub> from V<sub>CC</sub> to the collector, and the emitter goes to ground. I<sub>B</sub> is set by V<sub>CC</sub> and R<sub>B</sub> alone. Nothing senses I<sub>C</sub>, so nothing corrects it.
I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/R<sub>B</sub>,  I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub>,  V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>R<sub>C</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>CC</sub> is the supply in volts; V<sub>BE</sub> ≈ 0.7 V for a silicon transistor at room temperature; R<sub>B</sub> and R<sub>C</sub> are in ohms; I<sub>B</sub> and I<sub>C</sub> are in amperes. Germanium needs about 0.3 V; a Darlington pair about 1.4 V.

blocks.text: The stability factor is S = 1 + β. At β = 100, S = 101, the worst of any bias circuit: leakage is multiplied 101 times and doubling β doubles I<sub>C</sub>. β rises about 0.5% per °C; V<sub>BE</sub> falls about 2 mV per °C.
Use it for a hard-driven switch or the cheapest circuit, not a linear amplifier.

sections.h3: Collector feedback bias: the resistor watches the output

blocks.text: Return R<sub>B</sub> to the collector, not the supply. R<sub>C</sub> now carries I<sub>C</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>.
V<sub>CC</sub> = (I<sub>C</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>)R<sub>C</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>R<sub>B</sub> + V<sub>BE</sub>  →  I<sub>C</sub> = β(V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/(R<sub>B</sub> + (1+β)R<sub>C</sub>)
blocks.where: the first term is the drop across R<sub>C</sub> carrying both currents, the second is the drop across R<sub>B</sub>, and V<sub>BE</sub> ≈ 0.7 V. Solve with I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub>.

blocks.text: If I<sub>C</sub> rises, the R<sub>C</sub> drop rises, collector voltage falls, and less current enters the base through R<sub>B</sub>. That is negative feedback. The stability factor is S = (1+β)(R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>C</sub>)/(R<sub>B</sub> + (1+β)R<sub>C</sub>). With R<sub>B</sub> = 560 kΩ, R<sub>C</sub> = 2.2 kΩ and β = 100, S ≈ 73.
RB is an output-to-input path, so it lowers input resistance and gain; see Chapter 2.4.

sections.h3: Voltage divider bias: fix the base, let R_E set the current

blocks.text: R<sub>1</sub> from V<sub>CC</sub> to base, R<sub>2</sub> from base to ground, R<sub>E</sub> from emitter to ground, R<sub>C</sub> from V<sub>CC</sub> to collector. R<sub>E</sub> carries I<sub>E</sub>, turning voltage into current and fighting change: if I<sub>C</sub> rises, V<sub>E</sub> rises, V<sub>BE</sub> falls, and the transistor conducts less. Some syllabi call this self-bias or emitter bias.

V<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>),  V<sub>E</sub> = V<sub>B</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>,  I<sub>E</sub> = V<sub>E</sub>/R<sub>E</sub>,  I<sub>C</sub> ≈ I<sub>E</sub>,  V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>(R<sub>C</sub> + R<sub>E</sub>)
blocks.where: V<sub>CC</sub> is the supply in volts; R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>E</sub>, R<sub>C</sub> are in ohms; V<sub>BE</sub> ≈ 0.7 V; currents are in amperes. I<sub>C</sub> ≈ I<sub>E</sub> because α = β/(1+β) is within 1% of unity for β above 100.

blocks.text: The 10× rule: make the divider current through R<sub>2</sub> at least ten times I<sub>B</sub>. Then the base current barely loads the divider and the V<sub>B</sub> formula is good enough for an exam answer.

items: Choose V<sub>E</sub> about a tenth of V<sub>CC</sub>, so R<sub>E</sub> stabilises the point without eating the output swing.
V<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>E</sub> + 0.7 V; then R<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>B</sub>/(10I<sub>B</sub>) and R<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>B</sub>)/(11I<sub>B</sub>).
R<sub>C</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>CEQ</sub> − V<sub>E</sub>)/I<sub>CQ</sub>, with V<sub>CEQ</sub> near half of V<sub>CC</sub>.
Check that V<sub>CE</sub> stays above about 1 V, so the transistor never saturates on signal peaks.

blocks.text: S = (1+β)(1 + R<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>E</sub>)/(1+β + R<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>E</sub>) with R<sub>th</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> ∥ R<sub>2</sub>. The worked circuit gives S ≈ 8.5, and S falls towards 1 as R<sub>th</sub> becomes small against R<sub>E</sub>.

With CE across RE, the DC design is unchanged and the signal sees ground at the emitter. Remove CE and you have emitter-stabilized bias: same DC point, but gain drops to roughly RC/(RE + re). See Chapter 2.5.

examples.question: A voltage divider bias circuit uses V<sub>CC</sub> = 12 V, R<sub>1</sub> = 47 kΩ, R<sub>2</sub> = 10 kΩ, R<sub>C</sub> = 2.2 kΩ, R<sub>E</sub> = 1 kΩ, β = 100 and V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V. (a) Find the Q-point. (b) Check the 10× rule. (c) Find I<sub>C</sub> when β rises to 200 using the exact Thevenin solution, and compare with fixed bias.
steps: Neglect base current first. V<sub>B</sub> = 12 × 10/(47 + 10) = 2.105 V.
I<sub>E</sub> = 1.405 V/1 kΩ = 1.405 mA, so I<sub>C</sub> ≈ 1.405 mA.
V<sub>CE</sub> = 8.91 − 1.405 = 7.50 V. The transistor is active since V<sub>CE</sub> is well above 1 V.
Divider current I<sub>2</sub> = 2.105 V/10 kΩ = 210.5 µA. I<sub>B</sub> = 1.405 mA/100 = 14.05 µA. The ratio is 15, so the 10× rule holds.

Exact check: V<sub>TH</sub> = 2.105 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 47 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 8.246 kΩ, so I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>TH</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/(R<sub>th</sub> + (1+β)R<sub>E</sub>). At β = 100: I<sub>B</sub> = 1.405/(8.246 k + 101 k) = 12.86 µA, I<sub>C</sub> = 1.286 mA. At β = 200: I<sub>B</sub> = 1.405/(8.246 k + 201 k) = 6.72 µA, I<sub>C</sub> = 1.343 mA. That is a 4% rise; fixed bias would double I<sub>C</sub>.
examples.answer: I<sub>C</sub> ≈ 1.405 mA and V<sub>CE</sub> ≈ 7.50 V; the divider draws 210.5 µA against I<sub>B</sub> = 14.05 µA, and at β = 200 the exact I<sub>C</sub> is 1.343 mA, a rise of about 4% where fixed bias would double the current.
examples.check:
Vcc, R1, R2, RC, RE, VBE = 12.0, 47e3, 10e3, 2.2e3, 1e3, 0.7
VB = Vcc * R2 / (R1 + R2)
VE = VB - VBE
IE = VE / RE
IC = IE
VC = Vcc - IC * RC
VCE = VC - VE
Idiv = VB / R2
IB = IC / 100
print(round(VB, 3))
print(round(VE, 3))
print(round(IE * 1e3, 3))
print(round(VC, 2))
print(round(VCE, 2))
print(round(Idiv * 1e6, 1))
print(round(IB * 1e6, 2))
print(round(Idiv / IB, 1))
RTH = R1 * R2 / (R1 + R2)
for b in (100, 200):
    ib = (VB - VBE) / (RTH + (1 + b) * RE)
    print(round(b * ib * 1e3, 3))

traps: Using V<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) when I<sub>B</sub> is comparable to divider current. Check the 10× rule, or solve the Thevenin circuit.
Thinking V<sub>B</sub> sets the current. V<sub>E</sub> = V<sub>B</sub> − 0.7 V drives R<sub>E</sub>, so 0.1 V error in V<sub>B</sub> is about 7% error in I<sub>C</sub>.

In collector feedback, writing I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − 0.7)/R<sub>B</sub> and forgetting that R<sub>C</sub> carries I<sub>C</sub> + I<sub>B</sub> and that I<sub>C</sub> sets collector voltage.
Mixing kΩ with mA (they cancel and give volts) but pairing ohms with mA, which throws the answer off by 1000.
Calling a circuit with C<sub>E</sub> across R<sub>E</sub> 'emitter-stabilized' without saying for which quantity: the capacitor is open at DC and a short at signal frequency.

quiz.q: Which bias circuit has stability factor S = 1 + β?
quiz.a: Fixed bias, also called base bias.

quiz.q: In collector feedback bias, which terminal does the base resistor return to?
Explain in one sentence why collector feedback reduces drift of I<sub>C</sub>.
quiz.a: A rise in I<sub>C</sub> lowers collector voltage, reducing I<sub>B</sub> through R<sub>B</sub>, which pulls I<sub>C</sub> back down.

quiz.q: Why does the 10× rule matter before you use the divider formula?
quiz.a: The formula assumes I<sub>B</sub> does not load the divider. With divider current at least ten times I<sub>B</sub>, the loading error in V<sub>B</sub> is small enough to neglect in an exam answer.

quiz.q: Fixed bias: V<sub>CC</sub> = 10 V, R<sub>B</sub> = 470 kΩ, R<sub>C</sub> = 1 kΩ, β = 50, V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V. Find I<sub>C</sub> and V<sub>CE</sub>.
Voltage divider bias: V<sub>CC</sub> = 15 V, R<sub>1</sub> = 68 kΩ, R<sub>2</sub> = 12 kΩ, R<sub>E</sub> = 1.2 kΩ, V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V. Find V<sub>B</sub>, V<sub>E</sub> and I<sub>E</sub>.
A student builds the worked circuit and measures V<sub>B</sub> = 2.00 V instead of 2.105 V. Give the reason and the size of the effect.
quiz.a: Base current loads the divider, whose Thevenin resistance is R<sub>1</sub> ∥ R<sub>2</sub> = 8.246 kΩ. The drop is I<sub>B</sub>R<sub>th</sub> = 12.86 µA × 8.246 kΩ ≈ 0.106 V, so V<sub>B</sub> = 2.105 − 0.106 = 2.00 V. The 10× rule makes this the largest error in the approximate solution.

beyond: Not for the exam. Inside an integrated circuit, resistors are expensive and imprecise, so bias currents are copied from one reference transistor by current mirrors, and the reference is a bandgap circuit with a temperature coefficient of a few tens of ppm per °C. Discrete boards still use the divider because two resistors cost a few paise.
